title: Physical, Social, and Personal Determinants of the Perception of Crowding
research_question: To systematically understand how density interacts with certain social and personal factors to influence a person's behavior and perceptions about the environment, and to identify circumstances that sensitize individuals to the potential constraints of limited space.

participants.description: Students at the University of North Carolina, participating in same-sexed groups of eight, with an attempt to include only subjects unacquainted with each other.
participants.recruitment: Participated as part of a course requirement.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two experimental rooms (large and small), rectangular, with a one-way mirror. A movable wooden partition (8 ft high, ceiling extended 2 ft 4 in above) created the room sizes. Eight molded plastic chairs were arranged in the largest oval possible. Large room: 9 ft 11 in (3.02m) wide, 13 ft 6 in (4.11m) long, with 15 in (.39m) between adjacent chairs and 5 ft (1.55m) between chairs. Small room: 5 ft 7 in (1.70m) wide, 8 ft 1 in (2.46m) long, with chairs touching each other and 16 in (.41m) from front of one chair to front of opposite chair.

measures.instrument: 9-point semantic differential scales: 'physically uncomfortable-physically comfortable', 'cold-hot', 'not stuffy-stuffy'
9-point semantic differential scale: 'The other participants: passive-aggressive'
9-point semantic differential scale: 'How you felt during the game: passive-aggressive'

measures.instrument: 9-point semantic differential scales: 'unlikeable-likeable', 'bad-good', 'unfriendly-friendly' (for others); 'sociable, intimate, informal, friendly' (felt toward others)

mechanisms: Crowding is experienced as a syndrome of stress resulting from the disparity between one's supply of and demand for space.
Social circumstances (e.g., complex or competitive tasks) heighten an individual's demand for space.
Personal traits (e.g., impaired ability to interact smoothly) predispose individuals to feelings of restriction and crowding.
Laughter may operate as a coping response to perceived crowding stress.

Attribution theory explains perceived aggressiveness: noncorrespondent behavior (aggressiveness in cooperative task) is attributed to disposition, while correspondent behavior (aggressiveness in competitive task) is attributed to situational demands.
The general unpleasantness of the competitive condition may generalize to ratings of perceived crowding and restriction.

Males may attribute feelings of crowding more exclusively to physical features of the environment, while nonspatial sources of perceived crowding may be more salient for females due to their relatively greater favorableness toward smaller quarters.
Social interference (e.g., competition) makes the need to 'keep others at a distance' more salient, leading to perceived restriction and crowding.
implementation_implications: Social and personal variables mediate the perception of the environment and the experience of crowding, suggesting that the impact of spatial variables is determined through an interaction of physical, social, and personal factors.
Understanding crowding at the psychological level should have implications for dealing with crowding at the societal level.

limitations: The dissimilarities between the experimental situation and the urban environment limit the generality of findings to macro crowding phenomena (e.g., short exposure duration, awareness of eventual departure).
The potency of the room size manipulation may have 'swamped out' the effect of a competitive task set on the perception of crowding within the small room.

The experiment did not control for or manipulate the factor of time, making it impossible to ascertain whether the perception of crowding actually decreased over time within the small room, competitive condition.
It was impossible to ascertain whether increased laughter and noise reflected absence of crowding, a mode of coping, or a nonspatial source of heightened crowding (overstimulation).
Observer reliability figures may be somewhat elevated due to observers not being isolated from each other.
Experimenter effects were found for some measures (perceived quietness, name recall, number of jokes) which are not easily interpretable or uniquely relevant to crowding.

paper_metadata.title: Preferred Interpersonal Distances: A Global Comparison
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Preferred Interpersonal Distances: A Global Comparison
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Human spatial behavior has been the focus of hundreds of previous research studies. However, the conclusions and generalizability of previous studies on interpersonal distance preferences were limited by some important methodological and sampling issues. The objective of the present study was to compare preferred interpersonal distances across the world and to overcome the problems observed in previous studies. We present an extensive analysis of interpersonal distances over a large data set ( N = 8,943 participants from 42 countries). We attempted to relate the preferred social, personal, and intimate distances observed in each country to a set of individual characteristics of the participants, and some attributes of their cultures. Our study indicates that individual characteristics (age and gender) influence interpersonal space preferences and that some variation in results can be explained by temperature in a given region. We also present objective values of preferred interpersonal distances in different regions, which might be used as a reference data point in future studies.
